challenges.name: source-of-truth-quiz
challenges.title: Where do the scores live?
challenges.description: The state of Redis and PostgreSQL after the maintenance restart that emptied the leaderboard, and a proposal to fix it by turning on persistence.

questions.question:
The AI-written award path, deployed on 12 October:

async awardPoints(e: ScoreEvent) {
  await this.redis.zincrby("leaderboard:global", e.points, e.userId);
}

After the maintenance restart on 26 October:

$ redis-cli CONFIG GET save
1) "save"
2) ""
$ redis-cli CONFIG GET appendonly
1) "appendonly"
2) "no"
$ redis-cli ZCARD leaderboard:global
(integer) 0

codedev=# SELECT max(created_at) FROM score_events;
          max
------------------------
 2026-10-12 08:59:41+07

Statement: "The points awarded between 12 and 26 October cannot be recovered from Redis or from PostgreSQL."
questions.explanation: True. save "" disables RDB snapshots and appendonly no disables the AOF, so this Redis keeps data only in memory and a restart starts empty. The new awardPoints never writes score_events, which is why the newest row in PostgreSQL is from just before the deploy. The two weeks of points existed only in Redis memory, and that memory is gone; at best they can be re-derived from another log, such as the graded submissions, if one exists. The misconception is that Redis "has" the data because the leaderboard looked right for two weeks: a cache configured like this is a copy that can disappear at any time, so something durable must hold every event.

questions.question:
To prevent the next loss, a teammate proposes keeping awardPoints exactly as it is and changing only the Redis configuration:

appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec

The instance keeps maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, as it is also the cache for course pages, and a replica takes over automatically when the primary fails.

Statement: "With this configuration Redis can stay the only place where scores are written: a crash, a failover or memory pressure can no longer lose an awarded point."
questions.explanation: False. AOF with appendfsync everysec fsyncs about once per second, so a crash can lose roughly the last second of writes, which the Redis documentation states. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can promote a replica that has not received the last writes. And allkeys-lru may evict leaderboard:global itself when the course cache fills memory. The award path also has no event id, so a retried event is still counted twice. Persistence makes Redis restart faster and lose less; it does not turn a cache into the system of record. Write each score event to PostgreSQL first, idempotently by event id, and treat the sorted set as a copy you can rebuild. The misconception is that "persistent" means "durable and correct".

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-redis-source-of-truth
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: Redis as the source of truth
challenges.description:
The request sent to an AI coding assistant was: "GET /leaderboard is slow: it runs SUM(points) GROUP BY user_id over every score event on each request. Make the leaderboard fast." The assistant moved the scores into a Redis sorted set: awardPoints only runs ZINCRBY, top(n) runs ZREVRANGE and scoreOf runs ZSCORE. The page went from 900 ms to 4 ms and the pull request was merged. Two weeks later Redis restarted during maintenance (the instance runs without persistence): the leaderboard came back empty and every score was 0. Support also found learners whose score jumped when the grading worker retried a submission event it had already sent.

Fix LeaderboardService so that PostgreSQL holds every score event and Redis is only a fast copy:
- awardPoints(event) stores the event in PostgreSQL first with db.insertScoreEvent(event) (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING, which returns false when the event id is already stored). A repeated event id changes nothing and returns "duplicate". A new event returns "counted" and is added with ZINCRBY to the key leaderboard:global, but only if that key exists; when it is missing, the next read rebuilds it.
- top(n) and scoreOf(userId) answer from Redis. Only when leaderboard:global is missing do they rebuild it from PostgreSQL with one db.totalsByUser() query (then ZADD each total) before answering. A learner with no events has score 0.
- Keep the validation: an event without an eventId or userId, or whose points is not a whole number >= 1, returns "rejected" and is stored nowhere; top(n) with n not a whole number >= 1 returns an empty list.

Input (JSON on stdin): a list of steps: { "award": { "eventId", "userId", "points" } }, { "top": 3 }, { "score": "u_an" }, { "restart": true } (Redis loses every key) and { "check": true }. Output: one line per step, for example "award sub_1001 u_an +30 -> counted", "top 3 -> u_chi 40, u_an 30, u_binh 20" (ties: higher userId first, like Redis), "score u_an -> 30", and for check the events stored in PostgreSQL, the total per learner and how many times totalsByUser was queried. The public tests pass on the assistant's code; the hidden tests restart Redis, replay events and check PostgreSQL.
hints: If Redis lost every key right now, from which data could you compute each learner's score again? Does the assistant's code write that data anywhere?

Look at awardPoints first: what does it write, in which order, and what happens when the same eventId arrives twice? Then look at top and scoreOf: what do they do when leaderboard:global does not exist? FakeDb already has the two queries you need.

A similar case with other data: course ratings cached in a hash ratings:<courseId>. rate() first runs INSERT INTO ratings ... ON CONFLICT (user_id, course_id) DO NOTHING; only if a row was inserted and the hash exists does it run HINCRBY. getRating() checks EXISTS ratings:<courseId>; when it is missing it runs SELECT count(*), sum(stars) once, writes the hash, then answers from it.
